en.title: Yorùbá: the whole course
en.short: What the Yorùbá degree covers, how it is organised, its main areas and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Yorùbá is a Niger-Congo language spoken mainly in south-western Nigeria, with communities in Benin, Togo and the diaspora. The degree studies the language itself, its linguistics, its oral and written literature, and its culture. It is not only about learning to speak Yorùbá. It asks how the language is structured, how it is used in society, how its literature works, and how its ideas about the world are expressed.

The notes are in English. Yorùbá words appear with their tone marks and special letters because these are part of correct spelling. A student should be able to describe Yorùbá speech, texts and practices in clear English and to read Yorùbá material with care.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a BA in Yorùbá is usually a four-year full-time university programme, but entry mode and institution can change this. The National Universities Commission (NUC) regulates university programmes. Colleges of education award the Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE), and some universities teach Yorùbá within African or Nigerian languages departments. Master’s degrees usually take one to two years and may be MA or MPhil, depending on the institution.

In Benin and Togo, where Yorùbá is also spoken, programme names and awards differ. In Europe and North America, Yorùbá is often taught within African studies rather than as a full single-subject degree. Do not assume that one country’s pattern applies everywhere.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage begins with the language and its speakers, sounds and orthography, tone and syllable structure, then basic grammar of the noun phrase and of verbs and simple sentences. It adds foundations of oral literature, culture and worldview, and reading, writing and study skills.

The core stage moves through phonetics and phonology, morphology and word formation, syntax, semantics and pragmatics, dialectology and sociolinguistics, history and historical linguistics, lexicography, oral literature genres and performance, written literature in prose, poetry and drama, folklore and cultural studies, religion and philosophy, music, dance and performance, translation and interpreting, language policy and education, stylistics and discourse, creative writing, editing and media, and research methods and fieldwork.

The master’s stage adds advanced phonology and tone analysis, advanced syntax and semantics, theories of literary and cultural criticism, and research methods and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Treat tone marks and diacritics as part of spelling, not as decoration. Read aloud, listen to reliable recordings, and compare your pronunciation with a teacher or speaker. Keep a dictionary and note the tone pattern of new words.

Read Yorùbá texts from different genres. For literature, learn the genre, the performer or writer, the audience and the social setting. For linguistics, use examples and check them with a speaker. For fieldwork, ask permission, explain your purpose, and keep anonymity where promised. Do not rely only on English translations.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
A common mistake is dropping tone marks or writing Yorùbá as if it were English. Another is treating Yorùbá as one uniform language and ignoring dialect variation. Students also confuse oral and written literature, or describe a performance without its context.

In grammar, do not force English categories onto Yorùbá without evidence. In translation, avoid word-for-word renderings that lose tone, idiom or respect. In research, do not invent sources, quotations or statistics, and do not present one country’s language policy as universal. Check current official rules and your own handbook.

keyPoints: Yorùbá studies the language, its linguistics, literature and culture, not only conversation.
Tone marks and diacritics are part of correct Yorùbá spelling.
Degree lengths and awards differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
The course moves from sounds and basic grammar to core linguistics, literature, culture and research.
Study with real texts, speakers and recordings, and check examples rather than guessing.
Do not treat one dialect, country or policy as the whole of Yorùbá practice.

en.title: The Yorùbá Language and Its Speakers
en.short: Yorùbá, its speech communities in West Africa and the diaspora, and the terms language, dialect and standard.

sections.heading: The language
sections.text:
Yorùbá (Èdè Yorùbá) belongs to the Niger-Congo family, which covers most of Africa south of the Sahara. Within it, Yorùbá sits in the Volta-Niger branch and the Yoruboid group, with Igala and Itsekiri. It is unrelated to English but distantly related to Swahili.

A language is a system of sounds, words and grammar shared by a community. A speech community is the group who regularly use it, or one variety of it, to communicate.

sections.heading: Where it is spoken
sections.text:
The largest speech community is in south-western Nigeria: Lagos, Ogun, Oyo, Osun, Ondo and Ekiti, with speakers also in Kwara, Kogi and parts of Edo. Yorùbá is one of Nigeria’s three largest languages, with Hausa and Igbo, and the Constitution names it for possible use in the National Assembly alongside English.

Yorùbá and related Yoruboid varieties are also spoken in Benin, where the language and its speakers are often called Nàgó, and by smaller communities in Togo. The slave trade carried it to Cuba, Brazil and Trinidad, and large diaspora communities (speakers living outside the homeland) now live in Britain and the United States.

sections.heading: Language, dialect, standard
sections.text:
A dialect is a variety of a language spoken by a group defined by place or social background. Yorùbá has a chain of dialects, including Ọ̀yọ́, Ifẹ̀, Ìjẹ̀bú, Ẹ̀gbá, Ìjẹ̀ṣà and Èkìtì. Neighbouring dialects usually understand each other; distant ones may not.

A standard variety is the form fixed by writing, schooling and broadcasting. Standard Yorùbá grew in the nineteenth century, drawing heavily on Ọ̀yọ́, through the work of Samuel Ajayi Crowther and other missionaries. It is the form taught in schools.

sections.heading: Common misunderstandings
sections.text: Yorùbá is not one uniform speech. A Kétu speaker from Benin and an Ìbàdàn student may share the standard in class yet speak differently at home. Yorùbá is not a dialect of another language, and it is not spoken only in Nigeria or only by people of Yorùbá descent.

keyPoints: Yorùbá is a Niger-Congo language of the Volta-Niger branch, in the Yoruboid group with Igala and Itsekiri.
Its largest speech community is in south-western Nigeria, and it is also spoken in Benin, in Togo and in diaspora communities.
A dialect is a regional or social variety; a standard variety is the form fixed by writing, schooling and broadcasting.
Standard Yorùbá developed in the nineteenth century, drawing mainly on Ọ̀yọ́, through Crowther and other missionaries.
Yorùbá is a language in its own right, not a dialect of another language, and it is not spoken only in Nigeria.
Not all Yorùbá speakers speak alike: neighbouring dialects are usually mutually intelligible, distant ones may not be.

en.title: Sounds and Orthography of Yorùbá
en.short: The Yorùbá alphabet, vowels, nasal vowels, syllabic nasal, subdots, tone marks and spelling practice.

sections.heading: Alphabet and consonants
sections.text: Modern Yorùbá uses a Latin-based alphabet of 25 letters: a b d e ẹ f g gb h i j k l m n o ọ p r s ṣ t u w y. The letters c, q, v, x and z are not used. Gb is one consonant sound, made with the lips and back of the tongue together, not g plus b. Ṣ is pronounced like English sh. Read each word as written.

sections.heading: Vowels and subdots
sections.text: Yorùbá has seven oral vowels: a e ẹ i o ọ u. The subdot under e and o marks different vowels, not decorative marks. Ẹ is open, as in English bed; ọ is open, as in English law in many accents. The subdot under s gives ṣ, the sh sound. Without the subdot, e, o and s are different letters, so omitting it can change a word. Example: ọ̀mọ̀ means child; omo is not the same word.

sections.heading: Nasal vowels and syllabic nasal
sections.text: Five vowels can be nasal: an, ẹn, in, ọn, un. The n after the vowel shows that air passes through the nose; it is not a separate consonant there. A syllabic nasal is different: it is written n or ń and forms a syllable by itself. Tone marks are acute for high tone, grave for low tone, and no mark for mid tone. They are written on vowels and on syllabic n. Example: ilé (house) has high tone on the last syllable; ẹ̀kọ́ (lesson) has low tone on ẹ̀ and high tone on kọ́.

sections.heading: Reading, writing and errors
sections.text: Read simple words syllable by syllable and copy every mark. Practise: ilé, ọ̀mọ̀, ẹ̀kọ́, ṣé, gbà. Common errors are leaving out subdots, leaving out tone marks, and writing gb as two separate sounds. Another error is confusing a nasal vowel with a syllabic nasal. In writing, check each e, o and s for a subdot, and check each vowel and syllabic n for tone. A missing mark is a spelling mistake.

keyPoints: The Yorùbá alphabet has 25 letters and does not use c, q, v, x or z.
Gb is one consonant, and ṣ is pronounced like English sh.
The subdots in ẹ, ọ and ṣ mark different letters, not decoration.
Yorùbá has seven oral vowels and five nasal vowels written as vowel plus n.
A syllabic nasal is written n or ń and forms a syllable by itself.
Tone marks are acute for high tone, grave for low tone, and unmarked for mid tone; omitting them changes spelling.

en.title: Tone and Syllable Structure in Yorùbá
en.short: High, mid and low tone, tone marking, syllable types, meaning contrasts and nasalisation.

sections.heading: Three tones
sections.text: Yorùbá has three contrastive tones: high, mid and low. A tone is a pitch pattern on a syllable. High takes an acute accent (´), low a grave accent (`), and mid is left unmarked. Tone separates words with the same consonants and vowels. In ọkọ (husband) both syllables are mid. In ọkọ̀ (vehicle or canoe) the second syllable is low. In ọ̀kọ̀ (spear) both are low. Only pitch differs.

sections.heading: Marking tone
sections.text: Ordinary Yorùbá writing marks tone on vowels and on the syllabic nasal. Acute marks high, grave marks low, and mid is unmarked. So bàbá (father) has low then high. Tone marks belong in dictionaries, school books and formal writing. In informal messages many writers omit them, but learners should keep them: the same letters without tone may be read as another word. Tone can also be grammatical, for example in verb forms.

sections.heading: Syllables and nasals
sections.text: Most Yorùbá syllables are open: they end in a vowel, not a consonant. The main first-year types are V, a vowel alone, as in a; CV, consonant plus vowel, as in bà; and N, a syllabic nasal that forms a syllable by itself. Long vowels and nasal vowels add length or nasality but no final consonant. Nasalisation means air passes through the nose during a vowel. It is written with n after the vowel, as in inú (inside), where the first syllable is a nasal vowel. A syllabic nasal is different: it is a separate syllable and carries tone, as in ń lọ (is going), where ń is high.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Tone and syllable structure work together: a tone needs a syllable to carry it, and nasalisation can fill a syllable without adding a consonant. Read each syllable with its pitch, and keep tone marks in writing. Compare near neighbours; if pitch changes, meaning may change.

keyPoints: Yorùbá has three contrastive tones: high, mid and low.
High is marked with an acute accent, low with a grave accent, and mid is left unmarked.
Tone marks are part of correct spelling in formal Yorùbá writing.
The main syllable types are V, CV and the syllabic nasal N.
Nasal vowels are written with n after the vowel; a syllabic nasal is a separate tone-bearing syllable.
In ọkọ, ọkọ̀ and ọ̀kọ̀ the same consonants and vowels give different meanings because the tones differ.

en.title: Basic Grammar: The Noun Phrase
en.short: Nouns, pronouns, modifiers, possession and word order in simple Yorùbá noun phrases.

sections.heading: Head first
sections.text: A noun phrase is a group of words built around a noun, the head. In Yorùbá the head comes first and modifiers follow. Yorùbá has no definite article like English the; context or a demonstrative shows definiteness. So ilé can mean house or the house. Adding a modifier narrows the meaning: ilé ńlá is big house, ìwé tuntun is new book, and ọmọ kékeré is small child. In each example the first word is the head and the second word describes it.

sections.heading: Pronouns
sections.text: Pronouns can stand alone as noun phrases. The emphatic forms are èmi I, ìwọ you singular, òun he or she, àwa we, ẹ̀yin you plural, and àwọn they. Possessive forms follow the noun: mi my, rẹ́ your singular, rẹ̀ his or her, wa our, yín your plural, wọn their. Thus ọmọ mi is my child, ilé rẹ̀ is his or her house, and ilé wa is our house. The tone mark matters: rẹ́ and rẹ̀ are different words. Yorùbá possessive pronouns do not show gender.

sections.heading: Modifiers
sections.text: Common modifiers include adjectives, numerals and demonstratives. Adjectives follow the head: ilé ńlá big house. Numerals also follow: ìwé méjì two books, ọmọ mẹ́ta three children. Demonstratives follow the noun phrase: ilé yìí this house, ilé yẹn that house. A demonstrative can follow an adjective: ìwé tuntun yìí this new book. Do not translate English order word for word. English says my house, but Yorùbá says ilé mi, literally house my.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.text: To build a phrase, choose the head, then add modifiers in order. For my house use ilé + mi = ilé mi. For two books use ìwé + méjì = ìwé méjì. For this small child use ọmọ + kékeré + yìí = ọmọ kékeré yìí. To understand a phrase, find the head first, then ask what each following word adds. In ilé wa, ilé is the head and wa tells whose house it is. Read simple phrases aloud and check tone marks, because tone can change meaning.

keyPoints: Yorùbá noun phrases place the head noun before its modifiers.
Possessive pronouns follow the noun: ilé mi means my house.
rẹ̀ is third-person possessive and does not mark gender.
Demonstratives yìí and yẹn follow the noun: ilé yìí means this house.
Numerals follow the noun: ìwé méjì means two books.
Build and read phrases by finding the head first, then the modifiers.

en.title: Basic Grammar: Verbs and Simple Sentences
en.short: Yorùbá verb forms, aspect, mood, negation, simple sentence patterns, questions and commands.

sections.heading: Verbs and aspect
sections.text:
Yorùbá verbs do not change form for person or number: the same verb follows mo, o, ó, a, ẹ or wọ́n. Time is not shown by a verb ending. Context, time words and particles show it. Aspect shows how an action is viewed. The particle ń marks progressive action, ti marks completion, máa ń marks habit, and yóò marks future.

Examples: Mo lọ can mean I went or I go, depending on context. Mo ń lọ means I am going. Mo ti lọ means I have gone. Mo máa ń lọ means I usually go. Mo yóò lọ means I will go.

sections.heading: Mood and negation
sections.text:
Mood is the speaker’s attitude: a statement, a question or a command. The declarative statement is unmarked. Negation uses a negative particle and, for some persons, a special pronoun form. Mi ò lọ means I did not go. Kò lọ means he or she did not go.

Commands use the bare verb: Lọ means go. The negative command uses Má: Má lọ means do not go. Má wá means do not come. The verb itself does not change.

sections.heading: Simple sentences
sections.text:
The common simple pattern is subject + verb + object. Adé ra ìwé means Adé bought a book. With an aspect particle: Adé ń ra ìwé means Adé is buying a book. A verb may also take a direct object without a preposition: Mo fẹ́ omi means I want water.

The subject comes first. The object follows the verb. Yorùbá does not need a separate word for a or the in this pattern; context and the noun phrase carry that meaning.

sections.heading: Questions
sections.text:
Yes or no questions often begin with Ṣé: Ṣé ó lọ? means Did he go? Question words begin the question, usually followed by ni: Kí ni means what, Ta ni means who, Níbo ni means where, Báwo ni means how, and Ìgbà wo ni means when. Kí ni Adé fẹ́? means What does Adé want?

The question word does not change the verb. Word order and the question particle do the work.

keyPoints: Yorùbá verbs do not change form for person or number; time is shown by context, time words and particles.
Aspect is shown by particles such as ń for progressive, ti for perfect, máa ń for habitual and yóò for future.
Negation uses negative particles and special pronoun forms, as in Mi ò lọ and Kò lọ.
Simple sentences usually follow subject verb object order, as in Adé ra ìwé.
Yes or no questions often begin with Ṣé, and question words include Kí ni, Ta ni and Níbo ni.
Commands use the bare verb, and negative commands use Má, as in Lọ and Má lọ.

en.title: Foundations of Yorùbá Oral Literature
en.short: Proverbs, riddles, tales, praise poetry, narrative, performance, audience and transmission.

sections.heading: What oral literature is
sections.text: Oral literature is literature composed, performed and passed on by speech and memory rather than by writing. Its main Yorùbá genres include òwe (proverbs), riddles, àlọ́ (tales), oríkì (praise poetry) and ìtàn (narrative or history). These are not failed written texts. Written literature is composed in writing and usually read alone; oral literature lives in performance and can change with each telling. A written collection can preserve a version, but it cannot carry the whole event.

sections.heading: Proverbs and riddles
sections.text: Proverbs are short, fixed sayings that teach judgement. A speaker uses òwe to end an argument or advise without direct blame. Riddles are question-and-answer games: the poser gives a clue, the audience guesses, and the answer is checked publicly. They train attention and shared knowledge. At a family gathering, a grandmother may end an àlọ́ about greed with an òwe, and the children infer the moral.

sections.heading: Tales and praise poetry
sections.text: Àlọ́ are tales with characters, repetition and song. A performer may open with a formula, invite the audience to answer a refrain, and use voice, gesture and pauses. Oríkì praise poetry names a person, lineage, town or deity and recalls qualities and deeds; it is often sung or chanted. Ìtàn narrative can tell family, town or historical events. The same story may have many versions.

sections.heading: Performance and transmission
sections.text: Performance means the whole event: performer, audience, place, occasion, voice, drumming or clapping, and response. The audience is not passive; it may answer refrains, laugh, correct errors or ask for more. Transmission is by memory, imitation and apprenticeship, often within families or communities. Because no two performances are identical, scholars record variants and compare them. Oral and written literature can borrow from each other, but neither is superior.

keyPoints: Oral literature is composed and performed in speech and memory, not only written down.
Main genres include òwe (proverbs), riddles, àlọ́ (tales), oríkì (praise poetry) and ìtàn (narrative).
Performance includes performer, audience, occasion, voice and response; the audience is active.
Transmission is by memory, imitation and apprenticeship, so versions vary.
Written collections preserve versions but cannot replace the performance event.
Oral and written literature are different media; neither is superior.

en.title: Introduction to Yorùbá Culture and Worldview
en.short: Kinship, chieftaincy, festivals, naming, food, dress, values, religion, diversity and change in Yorùbá social life.

sections.heading: Kinship and chieftaincy
sections.text: Kinship is the system of relationships by birth, marriage and adoption. Yorùbá families often include an extended family and a lineage, a group tracing descent from a common ancestor. Age groups and associations also create social ties. Chieftaincy is a graded system of titled office. A king or ọba and chiefs may hold ritual, judicial or community roles. Their powers and titles differ by town and have changed under colonial rule, modern government and migration. Do not assume one rank or one ruler for all Yorùbá communities.

sections.heading: Festivals and life stages
sections.text: Festivals mark harvests, deities, Islamic and Christian calendars, and town history. Naming is a public event where relatives give names that may record circumstance, religion or family hope. Food and dress vary by town, religion, income and occasion. A festive cloth in one area may be ordinary elsewhere. These practices are not fixed: new foods, fabrics, music and media styles enter, and migrants adapt them.

sections.heading: Values and religion
sections.text: Commonly praised values include respect for elders, hospitality, communal help, honesty and hard work. They are ideals, not a description of every person. Religion shapes social life. Indigenous Yorùbá religion, Christianity and Islam all have many followers, and some people combine practices. Religious belonging affects naming, dress, food rules and festivals. Scholars describe Yorùbá worldview through ideas about the person, destiny, ancestors and moral order, but interpretations differ.

sections.heading: Diversity and change
sections.text: Yorùbá culture is internally diverse. Towns and subgroups have different histories, dialects and customs. The Atlantic slave trade, colonial rule, Christian and Muslim missions, wage labour, urbanisation, travel and broadcast media have all changed family life, chieftaincy, festivals and dress. A Lagos family may hold a naming ceremony with Muslim and Christian relatives while an elder keeps a hometown festival. Treat such a case as one example, not a rule for all Yorùbá people.

keyPoints: Yorùbá kinship includes extended family and lineage, and it varies by family and place.
Chieftaincy is a graded system of titled office whose powers differ by town and have changed over time.
Festivals, naming, food and dress are shaped by town, religion, income, occasion and change.
Commonly praised values such as respect, hospitality and communal help are ideals, not descriptions of every person.
Indigenous religion, Christianity and Islam all shape Yorùbá social life, and some people combine practices.
Yorùbá culture is internally diverse; avoid treating one town’s or one family’s practice as the rule for all.

en.title: Reading, Writing and Study Skills in Yorùbá
en.short: Reading, summary, essays, letters, punctuation, dictionary use, citation, sources and note-making.

sections.heading: Reading and summary
sections.text: Read a Yorùbá passage once for the general sense, then again with a pencil. Mark the main idea, the supporting points and any words you must look up. A summary restates the main points in your own words and in fewer words than the original. Keep the order of ideas and leave out examples unless they carry the argument. For example, a student given a page on market trade should write two or three sentences naming the main claim and reasons, not copy whole sentences.

sections.heading: Essays and letters
sections.text: An essay has an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion. State your position in the introduction, develop one point per paragraph, and support each point with evidence or an example. A formal letter follows a set layout: your address, the date, the receiver’s address, salutation, body, closing and signature. A letter to a head teacher asking for records, for example, should state who you are, what you need, why you need it and when. Keep the tone polite and direct.

sections.heading: Punctuation and dictionary
sections.text: Punctuation and paragraph breaks guide the reader: full stop, comma, question mark, colon and quotation marks. In Yorùbá writing, tone marks and sub-dots are part of spelling, so copy them exactly. A dictionary entry gives the headword, its part of speech, meaning and often an example. Use the guide words at the top of each page, and check the exact spelling before you quote a word. If a dictionary gives variants, record which one it uses.

sections.heading: Sources, honesty and notes
sections.text: Cite every book, article, website or interview you use. A citation normally gives author, title, year and publisher or URL, in the style your department requires. Academic honesty means not presenting another person’s words or ideas as your own; quote directly and mark the quotation, or paraphrase and cite. Use the library catalogue and reliable digital databases, and check whether a website has an author and date. For notes, write the source at the top, then short points in your own words. Review them soon.

keyPoints: Read a Yorùbá passage twice: first for sense, then for main points and unknown words.
A summary gives the main ideas in your own words and in fewer words.
An essay needs an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion; a formal letter follows a standard layout.
Punctuation and exact spelling, including tone marks, affect meaning and must be checked.
Cite every source and never present another person’s words or ideas as your own.
Good notes record the source first and use short points in your own words.

en.title: Yorùbá Phonetics and Phonology
en.short: Articulatory consonants and vowels, nasalisation, syllables, tone, harmony, processes and IPA transcription.

sections.heading: Consonants and vowels
sections.text: Consonants are described by place, manner and voicing. Yorùbá has stops /b t d k g/ and labial-velar /kp gb/, made with simultaneous closure at the lips and velum. It has fricatives /f s ʃ h/, nasals /m n/, approximants /j w l/, and a tap /ɾ/, written r. The letter ṣ is /ʃ/, and j is the affricate /dʒ/. The seven oral vowels are /i e ɛ a ɔ o u/; they differ by tongue height, backness and lip rounding. /ɛ/ and /ɔ/ are written ẹ and ọ.

sections.heading: Nasalisation and syllables
sections.text: Nasalisation means air flows through the nose. Yorùbá contrasts oral and nasal vowels; nasal vowels are written with n. A syllabic nasal is a separate syllable and can carry tone. Native syllables are V, CV or a syllabic nasal N; there are no consonant clusters. For example, ilé 'house' is /i.lé/, two syllables. ọ̀rẹ́ 'friend' is /ɔ̀.ɾɛ́/.

sections.heading: Tone and harmony
sections.text: Tone is pitch that distinguishes words. Yorùbá has high, mid and low tones, usually marked with acute, no mark and grave. Tone can be lexical and grammatical. Vowel co-occurrence is constrained by harmony: mid vowels pattern in two sets, often described by tongue root, and high vowels are neutral. Details vary by analysis.

sections.heading: Processes and transcription
sections.text: Common processes include nasal place assimilation, vowel elision, glide formation and tone spreading. In nasal assimilation a syllabic nasal takes on the place of articulation of the following consonant. In glide formation a high vowel before another vowel becomes /j/ or /w/. Transcribe with IPA and keep tone. Practice: ìwé 'book' /ì.wé/; ọ̀rẹ́ 'friend' /ɔ̀.ɾɛ́/; ilé 'house' /i.lé/. For each, mark syllables and tone, and say which processes, if any, apply.

keyPoints: Yorùbá has seven oral vowels and nasal vowels written with n.
Consonants include labial-velar /kp/ and /gb/, and r is usually a tap [ɾ].
Native syllables are V, CV or syllabic nasal N, with no consonant clusters.
Tone has high, mid and low levels; mid is usually unmarked.
Vowel harmony restricts which mid vowels co-occur; high vowels are neutral.
Transcribe with IPA and preserve tone marks, checking your course’s conventions.

en.title: Morphology and Word Formation in Yorùbá
en.short: Roots, affixes, reduplication, compounding, nominalisation, borrowing and ideophones in Yorùbá word structure.

sections.heading: Roots and affixes
sections.text:
Morphology studies how words are built from smaller meaningful parts. A root is the smallest part carrying core meaning, such as lọ, the verb root meaning go. An affix is a bound form, one that cannot stand alone, added to a root; a prefix comes before it, a suffix after it. Yorùbá has little inflection but uses derivation.

Roots are often monosyllabic, and tone belongs to the word: a different tone can make a different word. Productive affixes are limited. The prefix ì- turns a verb into a noun: lọ (go) becomes ìlọ (going). Suffixes are few, so compounding and reduplication do much of the work.

sections.heading: Reduplication and compounding
sections.text:
Reduplication repeats all or part of a word. Yorùbá uses it to form nouns, show plurality, repetition or intensity, and make expressive forms. The copy repeats the sounds of the base but follows fixed tone patterns; in the intensive form it takes a high tone even when the base does not, as in dùn (be sweet) giving dùndún (very sweet).

Compounding joins two or more roots or words into a new word. In ilé-ìwé (school), ilé means house and ìwé means book. The compound is a fixed noun whose meaning is more than the parts added together. Order is fixed, and tone and vowel elision (a vowel dropping at the join) must be learned word by word.

sections.heading: Nominalisation and borrowing
sections.text:
Nominalisation turns a verb, adjective or clause into a noun. Besides the ì- prefix, Yorùbá uses compounds and phrases as nouns. Analyse ìlọ as ì- plus lọ; analyse ilé-ìwé as a compound of two nouns.

Borrowing takes words from other languages and adapts them to Yorùbá sounds and syllable patterns. English motor gives mọ́tò (car): the final consonant is dropped and syllables stay open. Ideophones are vivid words depicting sound, movement or state; they often repeat syllables and use tone for effect.

To analyse a word, write it with all tone marks. Identify affixes, repeated material and compound members. Check whether it is borrowed and whether its tone pattern has changed. Do not force English categories onto Yorùbá.

keyPoints: Yorùbá morphology relies on roots, limited affixation, reduplication and compounding.
A root carries core meaning, while an affix is a bound form added to it.
The prefix ì- can nominalise a verb, as in lọ (go) to ìlọ (going).
Reduplication repeats material and follows fixed tone patterns, such as a high tone on the copy.
Compounds such as ilé-ìwé have fixed order and meaning beyond the parts.
Borrowed words are adapted to Yorùbá sounds, and ideophones are expressive tone-bearing words.

en.title: Yorùbá Syntax: Sentence and Clause Structure
en.short: Phrase structure, clause types, serial verbs, focus, relatives, negation and questions in Yorùbá.

sections.heading: Phrase and clause
sections.text: Yorùbá is basically SVO: the subject comes first, then the verb, then the object. The verb and most prepositions come before their complements, but nouns come before adjectives, possessors and the definite marker. A simple bracketed analysis of Adé gbé ìwé, “Adé carried a book”, is [S [NP Adé] [VP [V gbé] [NP ìwé]]]. A clause is a unit with a subject and predicate; a sentence may contain one clause or more. Main clause types are declarative, interrogative and imperative; clauses may be affirmative or negative. Complex sentences join clauses with conjunctions or embedding.

sections.heading: Serial verbs
sections.text: A serial verb construction (SVC) puts two or more verbs in one clause without a conjunction. The verbs share the subject, and usually the same aspect and polarity. Ó gbé ìwé wá means “he brought a book”, literally “he carried book came”. The second verb adds direction or result; SVCs also express instrument and benefaction. Because there is one clause, negation applies to the whole series, not to one verb alone.

sections.heading: Focus and relatives
sections.text: Focus highlights new or contrastive information. Yorùbá often fronts the focused phrase and marks it with ni: Adé ni ó gbé ìwé, “it is Adé who carried a book”. A relative clause modifies a noun and follows it, introduced by tí: ìwé tí Adé gbé, “the book that Adé carried”. Information structure also uses topic, the phrase the clause is about. Topic and focus are not the same: focus answers a question, topic sets the frame.

sections.heading: Negation and questions
sections.text: Negation usually places kò before the verb: Adé kò gbé ìwé, “Adé did not carry a book”. The negative marker interacts with aspect, pronouns and focus, so forms vary. Yes/no questions can begin with Ṣé: Ṣé Adé gbé ìwé? “Did Adé carry a book?” Wh-questions use a question word with ni and focus order: Tá ni ó gbé ìwé? “Who carried a book?” Tone and pronoun choice matter, and dialect forms differ.

keyPoints: Yorùbá basic order is SVO; verbs and prepositions precede complements, while noun modifiers follow the noun.
A clause has a subject and predicate; sentence types include declarative, interrogative and imperative; clauses are affirmative or negative.
In a serial verb construction, two or more verbs share one subject and one clause, with no conjunction.
Focus is marked by fronting and ni; relative clauses follow the noun and use tí.
Negation commonly uses kò before the verb, and yes/no questions can use Ṣé.
Information structure distinguishes topic from focus; word order and particles signal both.

en.title: Meaning in Yorùbá: Semantics and Pragmatics
en.short: Lexical meaning, polysemy, metaphor, idioms, proverbs, speech acts, politeness and context in Yorùbá.

sections.heading: Semantics and pragmatics
sections.text:
Semantics studies the conventional meaning of words and sentences. Pragmatics studies meaning in use: what a speaker intends and how a hearer works it out. Lexical meaning is the meaning a word carries in the dictionary. Polysemy is one word with several related senses, and context tells the hearer which sense is meant.

Yorùbá is a tone language, so a change of tone can change a word and its meaning. Tone marking in writing therefore reduces ambiguity.

sections.heading: Metaphor, idioms, proverbs
sections.text:
Metaphor speaks of one thing in terms of another by resemblance. An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is not the sum of its parts. A proverb is a short fixed saying from oral tradition that offers advice or judgement, often by allusion.

A speaker may use a proverb to advise or criticise without saying so directly, so the hearer needs shared cultural knowledge. The same proverb can be praise in one setting and rebuke in another.

sections.heading: Speech acts and politeness
sections.text:
A speech act is an action done in speaking, such as promising, warning or requesting. The theory separates the words uttered, the intended act and the effect on the hearer. An indirect speech act carries the intention in another form: "Is the door open?" may be a request to open it.

Politeness is the work speakers do to show respect and protect face, the public self-image. Yorùbá offers indirectness, titles, respectful vocabulary and proverbs; the forms vary by region, age and setting.

sections.heading: Context and inference
sections.text:
Context covers the setting, the relationship between speakers, the topic and shared history. The same sentence can be praise, teasing or a warning. Hearers draw implicatures: meanings suggested but not stated.

If a host says "There is food in the kitchen", the hearer may infer an invitation. Meaning depends on tone, situation and cultural knowledge together, not on the words alone.

keyPoints: Semantics studies conventional meaning; pragmatics studies meaning in use.
Polysemy is one word with several related senses, settled by context.
Yorùbá tone can change a word’s meaning, so tone marking matters in writing.
Proverbs advise or judge indirectly and depend on shared cultural knowledge.
A speech act is an action done in speaking, such as a request or promise.
Politeness protects face and is shown through indirectness, titles and respectful vocabulary.

en.title: Dialectology and Sociolinguistics of Yorùbá
en.short: Yorùbá dialect areas, standardisation, variation, code-switching, urban varieties and language attitudes.

sections.heading: Dialect areas
sections.text: Dialectology studies regional variation. Yorùbá is spoken across south-west Nigeria and nearby areas in many local varieties. Scholars often group them broadly, for example Ọ̀yọ́, Ẹ̀gbá, Ìjẹ̀bú, Èkìtì and Ọ̀ndọ́, but labels and boundaries vary. These varieties form a dialect continuum: neighbours understand one another fairly well, distant communities less. No variety is older or purer than another; each is a full system with its own sounds, words and tones.

sections.heading: Standard Yorùbá
sections.text: Standard Yorùbá is a codified variety used in schools, dictionaries, literature and media. It grew largely from Ọ̀yọ́ forms and spread through mission schools and publishing. Standardisation means selecting, writing down and spreading one variety; it does not make that variety linguistically better. A speaker may use standard forms in class and local forms at home, and both can be correct in their settings.

sections.heading: Switching and cities
sections.text: Code-switching is moving between languages or varieties. Yorùbá speakers switch between Yorùbá and English, and between standard and local forms. In cities, urban varieties mix Yorùbá with English, Nigerian Pidgin and other languages. A young speaker may begin in Yorùbá and insert an English word. This is not laziness; it follows social rules and can signal identity or humour.

sections.heading: Attitudes and multilingualism
sections.text: Language attitudes are people’s beliefs about a variety. Standard Yorùbá is often linked with education and prestige, local varieties with home and identity. Such attitudes can lead to unfair ranking, but linguists describe varieties without grading them. Many Yorùbá speakers are multilingual, using Yorùbá, English, Arabic or other Nigerian languages. A trader, a teacher and a radio presenter use different sets. Multilingualism is normal, not a failure of loyalty.

keyPoints: Dialectology studies regional variation; sociolinguistics studies language in its social setting.
Yorùbá local varieties form a dialect continuum, with understanding greatest between neighbours.
Standard Yorùbá is a codified variety spread by schools, missions and media, not a superior language.
Code-switching between Yorùbá, English and local varieties follows social rules and can signal identity.
Urban varieties are new ways of speaking, not broken Yorùbá.
Linguists describe varieties without ranking them, even when speakers hold strong attitudes.

en.title: History and Historical Linguistics of Yorùbá
en.short: Yoruboid relations, comparative and internal reconstruction, loanwords, early writing and orthography history.

sections.heading: Yoruboid and comparison
sections.text: Yorùbá belongs to the Yoruboid subgroup of the Volta-Niger branch of Niger-Congo. Close relatives include Igala and Itsekiri. The comparative method compares cognates, words in related languages that descend from one earlier word, to reconstruct Proto-Yoruboid. It looks for regular sound correspondences across many words, not for words that merely look alike. A single similar pair proves little; a repeated pattern is the evidence. The subgroup is defined by shared innovations, not geography.

sections.heading: Internal reconstruction and loans
sections.text: Internal reconstruction works inside one language. It compares alternating forms, such as fuller and contracted shapes, and removes regular changes to infer an older form. Loanwords show contact. English and Arabic are major sources for Yorùbá vocabulary; some Arabic words came through Islam and some through Hausa. Loans are adapted to Yorùbá sounds and tone. They show that contact happened, but not by themselves the exact date or direction.

sections.heading: Early writing and orthography
sections.text: Yorùbá was written in Ajami, Arabic script used for local languages, by some Muslim scholars before Latin script became dominant. In the nineteenth century missionaries, especially Samuel Ajayi Crowther, produced Latin-script vocabularies and grammars. Early systems differed in letters and tone marking. Standard orthography later settled on Latin letters plus ẹ, ọ, ṣ and tone marks, though practice still varies.

sections.heading: What evidence can show
sections.text: Historical evidence can show family relationships, reconstruct some earlier forms, and identify contact. It cannot give exact dates for split or borrowing, recover a full ancient culture, or prove every oral tradition. Written Yorùbá sources are relatively late and limited, so they document recent stages best. A claim is stronger when comparative, internal and written evidence agree. Dates from archaeology or oral history may help, but they are separate evidence.

keyPoints: Yorùbá belongs to the Yoruboid subgroup of Volta-Niger within Niger-Congo, with close relatives such as Igala and Itsekiri.
The comparative method reconstructs Proto-Yoruboid from regular cognate correspondences across related languages.
Internal reconstruction uses alternations within Yorùbá to infer older forms.
Loanwords from English and Arabic show contact but do not by themselves date it.
Yorùbá has Ajami and nineteenth-century Latin-script sources; standard orthography uses ẹ, ọ, ṣ and tone marks.
Historical linguistics can show relationships and contact, but not exact dates or a full ancient culture.

en.title: Yorùbá Lexicography and the Dictionary
en.short: Dictionary types, entry structure, tone marking, citation forms, corpora and judging Yorùbá dictionary entries.

sections.heading: Dictionary types
sections.text: Lexicography is the craft of making dictionaries. A dictionary may be monolingual, explaining Yorùbá in Yorùbá; bilingual or multilingual, pairing Yorùbá with English or another language; learner’s, aimed at students; historical, tracing older words; dialectal, recording regional usage; specialised, covering terms in one field; or electronic, searchable and updatable. Each type serves a different user, so no single dictionary answers every question. A good dictionary states its purpose, its sources and its spelling policy.

sections.heading: Inside an entry
sections.text: An entry normally has a headword, pronunciation and tone, part of speech, numbered senses, examples, idioms, cross-references and sometimes etymology. The citation form is the form chosen as the headword. Yorùbá dictionaries usually cite nouns with their initial vowel and verbs in the simple stem, but each dictionary should say what it does. Tone marking is essential: high tone takes an acute accent, mid tone is usually unmarked, low tone takes a grave accent, and the letters ẹ, ọ and ṣ carry subdots. For example, ọkọ̀ (vehicle) must not be merged with ọkọ́ (husband).

sections.heading: Corpora and problems
sections.text: A corpus is a collected body of written or spoken Yorùbá used to find real examples, frequency and collocations. A concordance shows a word in its surrounding lines. Corpus evidence helps lexicographers choose senses and write natural examples. Problems include inconsistent tone and diacritics in digital text, dialect variation, deciding the standard form, homographs, multiword expressions, neologisms and loanwords. Sense discrimination is hard because one word may have many related meanings.

sections.heading: Exercises
sections.text: Exercises: compare two entries for the same word and ask which gives clearer senses, examples and tone. Check every accent and subdot. Identify the citation form of a noun and a verb. Trace one example to a corpus line. Judge whether an idiom is listed under the right headword. Decide how to enter a multiword expression. Ask whether the dictionary tells the user its policy on tone, dialect and sources.

keyPoints: Lexicography is the craft of making dictionaries, and different dictionary types serve different users.
An entry usually includes a headword, tone, part of speech, senses, examples and cross-references.
Yorùbá tone marks and subdots must be printed accurately because they distinguish words.
Citation form is the headword form; dictionaries should state whether nouns keep initial vowels and verbs use stems.
Corpora supply real examples and frequency, but tone inconsistency and dialect variation are practical problems.
Judge an entry by clarity, accuracy, examples, sense division and stated policy.

en.title: Yorùbá Oral Literature: Genres, Performance and Recording
en.short: Proverbs, riddles, tales, praise poetry, incantation and narrative in performance and recording.

sections.heading: Genres and functions
sections.text: Yorùbá oral literature is spoken, sung or chanted before an audience. Proverbs (òwe) are short, fixed and allusive; speakers use them to teach, argue and sum up. Riddles test wit through metaphor. Tales (àlọ́) mix narration, song and audience chorus, and often end with a moral. Praise poetry (oríkì) names a person, lineage or town through epithets and parallel lines. Incantation (òfò̀) uses fixed, rhythmic words believed to act on the world. Historical and hunters’ chants belong here, though local forms vary.

sections.heading: Performance and formula
sections.text: Performance context shapes meaning: occasion, place, audience, performer’s status, gesture, music and tone of voice all matter. Many genres use call and response, repetition and formulaic language. A formula is a ready-made phrase or pattern, such as a stock opening, a praise epithet or a repeated chorus. It aids memory and lets the performer vary detail while keeping the frame. The same tale told at a funeral, a naming ceremony or a school contest is not the same text.

sections.heading: Recording and transcription
sections.text: Recording turns a performance into a document, but it also changes it. A microphone may make a performer more formal, shorten a tale or repeat a favourite song for the recorder. The recordist should note date, place, performer, audience, language variety and consent. Transcription must mark tone, because tone distinguishes words in Yorùbá; it should also mark pauses, line breaks, song, chorus, overlap and laughter. A clean written text is an interpretation, not the performance itself.

sections.heading: Analysis and variation
sections.text: Analysis compares recordings and transcripts. Ask who performs, for whom, and why. Look for formulae, proverbs, parallel lines and changes between versions. In a small case, a student records the same grandmother telling an àlọ́ twice. In the first version the audience joins the chorus; in the second she shortens the opening and adds a proverb about a quarrel in the yard. Neither version is the “correct” one. The archive should keep both, with context, so later readers can study how performance changes.

keyPoints: Oral genres include proverbs (òwe), riddles, tales (àlọ́), praise poetry (oríkì) and incantation (òfò̀).
Performance context, audience, gesture and music shape the meaning of an oral text.
Formulaic language gives memory and frame while allowing variation.
Transcription must mark tone, pauses, song, chorus and audience response.
Recording and editing change performance, so keep context and consent notes.
Compare multiple versions rather than treating one transcript as the correct text.

en.title: Yorùbá Written Literature: Prose, Poetry and Drama
en.short: Growth of Yorùbá novels, poetry and drama, with technique, themes, oral sources and publishing.

sections.heading: Growth and publishing
sections.text: Yorùbá written literature grew from nineteenth-century missionary literacy, Bible translation, newspapers. Early authors wrote for mission and colonial readers; later writers used local publishers, university presses and self-publishing. D. O. Fagunwa’s forest-adventure novels are often named as a foundation of Yorùbá prose. Drama grew through church and school performances, travelling theatre and published plays. Poetry moved from hymn and newspaper verse into collections shaped by oral praise poetry and chant. Publishing involves editing, copyright, printing and distribution. Readership is often small beside English, so subsidy and school adoption matter.

sections.heading: Narrative technique
sections.text: Prose fiction uses plot, character, setting, point of view and style. Plot is the arranged sequence of events; point of view is who tells the story. Yorùbá novels often keep an oral narrator who addresses readers, digresses, and quotes proverbs and songs. This creates intimacy and moral comment, but may slow suspense. Characterisation may use type and praise name. Style includes proverbs, ideophones (vivid words that imitate sounds or suggest sensations), repetition, parallelism and dialogue. Themes include tradition and modernity, colonial change, religion, family, migration, corruption and gender. Concrete case: compare a novel’s opening with a folktale opening. Note the formula, the narrator’s aside and the first proverb, then ask what each does.

sections.heading: Poetry and drama
sections.text: Written poetry uses line, stanza, rhythm, image and tone. It may adapt oral forms such as praise poetry, chant, song and proverb. Drama is built for performance: dialogue, conflict, stage directions, characters and audience. Yorùbá drama often joins speech with music, dance and spectacle. Describe form before meaning: line pattern, stanza shape, dramatic structure and song. Then link form to theme and context.

sections.heading: Writing about works
sections.text: Begin with close reading: quote briefly, preserve tone marks and special letters, and cite the edition. Summarise only enough plot to support analysis. Discuss voice, style, theme and oral source together. Ask how publication shaped the text: serialisation, censorship, school editing or translation. Compare oral and written versions without assuming one is purer. Check names, titles and dates against the book itself.

keyPoints: Yorùbá written literature grew from missionary literacy, newspapers, school readers and later local publishing.
D. O. Fagunwa’s adventure novels are often treated as a foundation of Yorùbá prose.
Yorùbá novels often use an oral narrator, proverbs, songs and digression to create intimacy and moral comment.
Written poetry adapts oral praise, chant and song, while drama joins dialogue with music, dance and spectacle.
Publishing includes editing, copyright, printing and distribution, and readership is often small beside English.
When writing about a work, use close reading, preserve tone marks, cite the edition and relate form to theme and context.

en.title: Folklore and Cultural Studies in Yorùbá
en.short: Folklore theory, collecting and classifying proverbs, riddles and tales, festivals, material culture, heritage and research ethics.

sections.heading: What folklore is
sections.text:
Folklore is expressive culture passed on within a group: tales, proverbs, riddles, songs, dance, crafts and festivals. A folk group is any group sharing traditions. Older collectors treated folklore as survivals from the past. Modern study stresses performance and context: who tells what, to whom, when and why.

A proverb is a short fixed saying used to make a point. A riddle is a question with a conventional answer. A tale is a narrative told to teach or entertain. All three are social acts, so the occasion matters as much as the words.

sections.heading: Collecting and classifying
sections.text:
Collect in natural settings. Record exact wording, tone marks, a translation, the performer, age, place, date and occasion. Keep each variant separate; a printed text does not replace a spoken one.

Classify proverbs by theme, key word, first line or use. Classify riddles by answer and structure. Classify tales with motif or tale-type indexes such as the Aarne-Thompson-Uther index. These indexes were built mainly from European material, so use them as tools and record local categories too.

Case: a student hears a proverb in Ibadan, notes it was used in a quarrel, later finds a printed variant, and files both as variants.

sections.heading: Festivals and material culture
sections.text: Festivals are recurring public events with ritual, music, dress, food and trade. They mark calendars, honour deities or ancestors, and renew community ties. Material culture means the objects people make and use: textiles, beadwork, pottery, carving, buildings and tools. Heritage is the culture a group or state chooses to preserve and pass on. Preservation always involves selection, so ask who decides.

sections.heading: Ethics in research
sections.text: Researchers need informed consent: explain the purpose, ask permission, and respect refusal. Agree how names, recordings and images will be used, and honour restrictions on secret or sacred knowledge. Pay performers fairly and give copies back. Cite collaborators as knowledge holders, not only as sources. Check current university ethics rules, which differ by country.

keyPoints: Folklore is expressive culture studied in performance and context, not only as old texts.
Record exact wording, tone marks, performer, place, date and occasion for every item.
Proverbs, riddles and tales can be classified by theme, structure or use, and by motif indexes.
Festivals and material culture carry identity and must be studied with their makers.
Heritage is selected and managed, so ask who decides what is preserved.
Informed consent, respect for sacred knowledge and fair credit are basic research duties.

en.title: Yorùbá Religion and Philosophy
en.short: Traditional Yorùbá religion, personhood and destiny, ethics, Ifá divination, and encounters with Islam and Christianity.

sections.heading: Religion and deities
sections.text: Traditional Yorùbá religion has no single founder, central scripture or authority. Practice varies by town, lineage and family. Many accounts describe one supreme being, Olódùmarè, often approached through intermediaries called òrìṣà. Other accounts stress the powers of particular places and ancestors. Scholars debate whether the category “religion” fits these practices neatly, and whether the tradition is better called monotheistic, polytheistic or both. Treat these as beliefs, not settled facts.

sections.heading: Person and destiny
sections.text: Ideas of the person include orí, the head, which can mean the physical head and an inner head linked to destiny. Ipín means a portion or allotted destiny. Some tell of choosing a destiny before birth; others stress that character, ìwà, and ritual action can shape a life. This is debated, not a single doctrine. A case: a family may consult a diviner when a child is sick, then discuss whether the illness calls for medicine, ritual or moral repair. The case shows how destiny language can guide action without fixing it in advance.

sections.heading: Ethics and Ifá
sections.text: Yorùbá ethics often centres on good character, respect for elders, community and balance. Ifá is a divination system with a large corpus of Odù, signs or chapters, each containing verses and prescriptions. A Babaláwo, a trained diviner, casts the divination instrument and interprets the Odù for the client. Ifá is used to seek knowledge about illness, conflict, marriage or travel, and to prescribe offering or conduct. It is not simply fortune-telling. Some treat it as religion, others as philosophy, literature or medicine; these views can overlap.

sections.heading: Islam and Christianity
sections.text: Islam and Christianity reached Yorùbá communities in Nigeria and neighbouring areas over a long period. Many Yorùbá people are Muslim or Christian while keeping some traditional practices, such as naming ceremonies or respect for ancestors. Scholars disagree about how to describe this: adaptation, coexistence, syncretism or conversion. Some leaders condemn mixing; others see continuity. The debate is partly about what counts as “traditional” and who has authority to define it.

keyPoints: Traditional Yorùbá religion has no single founder or central scripture, and practice varies by place and lineage.
Olódùmarè is often described as a supreme being approached through òrìṣà, but scholars debate how to classify the tradition.
orí and ipín are key ideas about the person and destiny, while ìwà (character) is central to ethics.
Ifá divination uses Odù and trained Babaláwo to interpret signs and prescribe conduct or offering; it is not only fortune-telling.
Yorùbá people have long interacted with Islam and Christianity, and scholars disagree whether the result is adaptation, coexistence, syncretism or conversion.
Internal debates exist over destiny, the category of religion, and the authority to define tradition.

en.title: Yorùbá Music, Dance and Performance
en.short: Vocal and instrumental genres, talking drum, praise singing, dance, theatre, popular music and performance analysis.

sections.heading: Genres and occasions
sections.text: Yorùbá music and dance are social arts tied to naming, marriage, burial, festival, worship and entertainment. Vocal genres include oríkì, praise poetry that names people and deeds; hunters’ chant; religious song; and work song. Instrumental ensembles combine drums, metal gongs, rattles and flutes. The dùndún talking drum is widely known; bàtá belongs to another drum tradition. Repertories vary by town, family and purpose, so note the occasion and performers, not only the sound.

sections.heading: Talking drum and praise
sections.text: Drum language uses drum pitch to carry phrases. On the dùndún, the player squeezes tension cords to change pitch, following Yorùbá tones. Skilled drummers quote proverbs, praise names and signals, but meaning depends on formula, context and audience knowledge; not every rhythm is speech. Praise singing, often using oríkì, names lineage, character and achievement and often alternates with drumming. In a small case, a drummer at a family ceremony plays a praise phrase for the hosts, a singer answers, and the audience responds. The analyst records the phrase, asks its meaning, and notes when each answer comes.

sections.heading: Dance, theatre, popular music
sections.text: Dance carries meaning through steps, posture, gesture and costume. It may mark gender, status, deity or event, and dancers often answer drum calls. Theatre joins music, dance and drama; twentieth-century travelling theatre and folk opera brought Yorùbá stories to large audiences. Popular music includes jùjú and fújì, which mix praise singing, guitars, drums and keyboards. Recording, radio and clubs change how performances are made and heard. Ask who performs, pays and listens.

sections.heading: Analysing performance
sections.text: Performance analysis starts with description. Note the event, place, date, purpose, performers, audience, instruments, language, structure, call and response, rhythm, dance, dress and payment. Record audio or video only with consent, and make time-coded notes. Interview performers about names, texts and choices, and compare several performances. Treat one event as one example, not the whole tradition. This links sound to social meaning and tests claims about genre, identity and change.

keyPoints: Yorùbá performance genres are tied to social and religious occasions, and repertories vary by place and purpose.
The dùndún talking drum changes pitch by tension cords and can carry formulaic phrases, but meaning depends on context.
Oríkì praise singing names lineage and achievement and often alternates with drumming.
Dance and theatre combine movement, music and drama, and popular styles such as jùjú and fújì reshape older forms.
Performance analysis describes participants, setting, structure, language and response, and compares several events.
Record and interview only with consent, and treat one performance as one example, not the whole tradition.

en.title: Translation and Interpreting between Yorùbá and English
en.short: Theory, equivalence, tone, culture, terminology, interpreting practice and ethics in Yorùbá-English work.

sections.heading: Theory and equivalence
sections.text: Translation transfers written meaning; interpreting transfers spoken or signed meaning in real time. Theory asks what should stay the same. Formal equivalence keeps the source form close. Dynamic equivalence aims for the same effect on the target reader. Eugene Nida described these ideas. A translator first identifies the function of the text: information, persuasion, ritual or art. The choice of strategy follows from that function, the audience and the brief.

sections.heading: Tone and culture
sections.text: Yorùbá is a tonal language, and standard orthography marks tone. A missing or changed tone mark can change a word, so copy tone marks exactly and check them. Culture adds meaning that a literal rendering may lose. Proverbs, greetings, respect terms, names and religious language often carry implied social relations. A translator may keep the image, explain it, or replace it with a target-culture equivalent. Each choice has a cost. For example, a proverb used to open a speech may need a short explanation in English if no close proverb exists.

sections.heading: Terminology and interpreting
sections.text: Terminology work builds a consistent glossary: source term, agreed target term, definition, example and source. For new technical ideas, translators may borrow a word, translate its parts literally, extend an old word, or coin a new one, then record the decision. Interpreting practice includes consecutive interpreting, where the interpreter speaks after segments and may take notes, and simultaneous interpreting, which follows the speaker closely. Preparation matters: read the agenda, confirm names and titles, and agree on mode and seating.

sections.heading: Ethics and problems
sections.text: Professional ethics require accuracy, confidentiality, impartiality, competence and disclosure of conflicts. Interpreters should not add advice or omit uncomfortable content. Common problems include false friends, that is, similar-looking words with different meanings; idioms; proverbs; honorifics; dialect variation; code-switching; rapid numbers; and poor sound. Yorùbá-English work also faces uneven dictionaries and spelling variation. When meaning is uncertain, ask the speaker or client, note the uncertainty, and avoid guessing.

keyPoints: Translation is written; interpreting is spoken or signed and immediate.
Formal equivalence keeps source form; dynamic equivalence aims for equivalent effect.
Yorùbá tone marks must be preserved because tone can change meaning.
Cultural terms and proverbs may need explanation or adaptation, not blind literalism.
Terminology glossaries keep technical terms consistent and record decisions.
Ethics require accuracy, confidentiality, impartiality, competence and disclosure of conflicts.

en.title: Yorùbá in Education and Language Policy
en.short: Covers mother-tongue teaching, curriculum, teacher training, orthography and policy in Nigeria and nearby countries.

sections.heading: Mother-tongue education
sections.text: Mother-tongue education means teaching early subjects in the learner’s first language, often with a planned move to a second language. It can improve comprehension and participation in multilingual classes. Language policy is the set of official decisions about which languages are used in schools and public life. Language-in-education planning turns policy into curriculum, materials and teacher deployment. A policy may allow Yorùbá as an early medium and as a later subject, but classroom practice can differ.

sections.heading: Curriculum and teachers
sections.text: The school curriculum sets what is taught, how it is assessed and what resources are needed. Yorùbá as a school subject joins language, literature and culture, so teachers need grammar, composition, oral literature and cultural knowledge. Teacher training should cover reading and writing methods, lesson planning, assessment and correct use of the orthography. Colleges of education and universities prepare teachers, but shortages of trained teachers and textbooks are common. A school may have a Yorùbá-medium policy for early classes, yet use English because parents expect it and examinations reward it.

sections.heading: Orthography in schools
sections.text: Orthography is the accepted writing system of a language. Standard Yorùbá uses the Latin alphabet with the letters ẹ, ọ and ṣ, and tone marks. Schools must teach these marks because they carry meaning; omitting them can make a word wrong or ambiguous. Textbooks, examination papers and keyboards should support the full orthography. Teachers should mark tone and subdots consistently.

sections.heading: Nigeria and neighbours
sections.text: Nigeria’s National Policy on Education has supported mother-tongue or community-language instruction in early primary, with English as a subject, but implementation varies by state, school and period. Yorùbá is also spoken in parts of Benin and Togo, where French and national-language policies shape schooling differently. Policy differs by country and changes, so students should check current official documents, such as national education policies and examination syllabuses.

keyPoints: Mother-tongue education teaches early subjects in the learner’s first language and can improve comprehension.
Language-in-education planning turns policy into curriculum, materials and teacher deployment.
The Yorùbá school curriculum joins language, literature and culture, and needs trained teachers.
Standard Yorùbá orthography uses ẹ, ọ, ṣ and tone marks, which schools must teach and mark consistently.
Nigeria’s National Policy on Education has supported early mother-tongue or community-language instruction, but practice varies.
Policy differs by country and changes, so check current official documents for Nigeria, Benin, Togo and other settings.

en.title: Stylistics and Discourse Analysis in Yorùbá
en.short: Style, discourse markers, conversation, oral narrative, rhetoric and corpus study in Yorùbá.

sections.heading: Style and context
sections.text: Stylistics studies the choices a writer or speaker makes and their effects. In Yorùbá, choices include tone, repetition, proverbs, address forms, sentence length and code-switching, moving between languages. Discourse analysis studies language in use, beyond the sentence: who speaks, to whom, where and why. The same sentence can praise, tease or accuse depending on context. A stylistic feature is not decorative only; it guides interpretation. A praise singer may repeat a name and phrase. Repetition builds emphasis, while the occasion tells hearers the words are praise, not insult.

sections.heading: Markers and talk
sections.text: Discourse markers are words or phrases that signal how ideas connect, such as ṣùgbọ́n (but), nítorí pé (because) and nígbà tí (when). They help listeners follow contrast, reason and time. Conversation analysis examines turn-taking, adjacency pairs such as question and answer, repair, fixing misunderstanding, and preference for agreement. In Yorùbá talk, age, status and polite address can shape who speaks first and how disagreement is phrased. If a speaker says a plan is good, then adds ṣùgbọ́n, hearers expect a limitation. Remove the marker and the limitation may seem abrupt.

sections.heading: Narrative and rhetoric
sections.text: Oral narrative structure can be described with Labov’s parts: abstract, orientation, complicating action, evaluation, resolution and coda (closing). Many Yorùbá àlọ́ and ìtàn use these moves, but not every performance follows the order. Evaluation tells hearers how to judge the action. Rhetoric is the art of persuasion. Yorùbá speakers use proverbs, parallelism, balanced phrasing, repetition and praise names to persuade or hold attention. In oríkì, compressed praise phrases carry history and value. Form and context together shape meaning.

sections.heading: Corpus study
sections.text: A corpus is a collected body of texts used for systematic study. A Yorùbá corpus may include novels, plays, newspapers, interviews and transcribed oral performances. Researchers standardise spelling and tone marks, annotate genres and speakers, then count and compare patterns. Corpus findings can test impressions, but poor transcription or mixed spelling systems can distort counts. Report the source, size and annotation rules.

keyPoints: Stylistics explains how formal choices such as tone, repetition and proverbs create effects.
Discourse analysis studies language in context, including speakers, purposes and social relations.
Discourse markers such as ṣùgbọ́n and nítorí pé guide how listeners connect ideas.
Conversation analysis examines turn-taking, adjacency pairs and repair in talk.
Oral narratives often use Labov’s parts, but not every Yorùbá performance follows that order.
Corpus studies need consistent spelling and tone marking, or counts can mislead.

en.title: Creative Writing, Editing and Media in Yorùbá
en.short: Writing fiction, poetry and drama in Yorùbá, then editing, publishing, broadcast and online media, and ethics.

sections.heading: Writing in Yorùbá
sections.text:
Fiction builds character, setting and plot. Poetry compresses language and uses rhythm, image and sound. Drama is written for performance, so dialogue and stage directions guide actors and readers. In Yorùbá, read each draft aloud to test natural speech, and keep a style sheet for names, spellings and punctuation.

A case: Amina writes a short story for a campus magazine in Ibadan. She checks that every tone mark and mark below a letter is correct, that a proverb is credited, and that the ending is clear when read aloud. Chidi, the editor, asks her to cut a long sentence.

sections.heading: Editing and proofreading
sections.text:
Substantive editing, which reshapes the piece, asks whether structure, character, argument and audience work. Copy editing then fixes grammar, word division, consistency and Yorùbá tone marks and marks below letters. Proofreading is the last check of the finished text or page against the agreed version.

An editor should query, not silently rewrite, when meaning is unclear. Keep a style sheet and record decisions. Check quotations, names, dates and proverbs. If a proverb is attributed, confirm the source or remove the attribution.

sections.heading: Publishing and media
sections.text:
Publishing may be through a press, a journal, a school, or self-publishing. Read the contract, keep copies, and check proofs before printing. For radio and television, adapt the text to time and to the ear: shorter sentences, clear pronunciation, and a reader who understands the tone marks.

Online media adds headlines, tags, links, images and fast correction. A misleading headline weakens trust. Keep an update note when facts change.

sections.heading: Ethics and public writing
sections.text:
Public writing carries duties: accuracy, fairness, consent, privacy and respect. Do not invent quotes, proverbs or sources. Credit other people’s work and ask permission before using protected text, images or recordings. Label opinion as opinion, and correct errors openly.

Rules on copyright, defamation (harmful false statements) and broadcasting differ by country and change over time. Check the current law and the publisher’s or station’s guidelines before you publish.

keyPoints: Fiction, poetry and drama each make different demands on a Yorùbá writer.
Reading a draft aloud helps test natural speech, rhythm and clarity.
Substantive editing, copy editing and proofreading are separate stages.
Yorùbá editing checks tone marks, marks below letters, word division and consistency.
Radio, television and online media require adaptation to time, ear and screen.
Ethics require accuracy, consent, credit and open correction.

en.title: Research Methods and Fieldwork in Yorùbá Studies
en.short: Choosing topics, reviewing literature, fieldwork, consent, transcription, analysis and archiving.

sections.heading: Topic and review
sections.text: Choose a topic that is narrow, feasible and ethical. Turn it into a research question, for example: How do radio presenters in one town adapt Yorùbá proverbs for young listeners? Check time, access, language skills and costs. A literature review is a critical summary of existing work, not a list. Search books, journals and archives, judge each source, and state the gap your project fills.

sections.heading: Fieldwork and consent
sections.text: Elicitation means asking speakers for words, sentences or stories under controlled prompts; also collect natural speech where possible. Record with a good microphone, note date, place and speakers, and back up files daily. Informed consent means explaining the purpose, risks, use and storage of data, then obtaining voluntary agreement, with permission to withdraw. Protect confidentiality by anonymising names unless the speaker agrees otherwise. Community and institutional rules vary by country; follow your ethics committee and any local protocol.

sections.heading: Transcription and annotation
sections.text: Transcribe in the agreed orthography, marking tone and special letters carefully; if unsure, ask the speaker. Use time codes and consistent conventions. Annotation adds information: translation, gloss, speaker details, genre, setting and tags. Keep a data key. For literature or culture projects, record performances and note audience, occasion and variants. Check transcripts with speakers where possible.

sections.heading: Analysis and archiving
sections.text: Qualitative analysis codes text into themes; quantitative analysis counts. Example: 40 interviews are coded for favourite Yorùbá media. 25 mention radio and 15 mention television. Radio = 25 ÷ 40 = 0.625, or 62.5%; television = 15 ÷ 40 = 37.5%. Report the base and avoid overgeneralising. Archive recordings, transcripts and metadata in open or stable formats, with access levels and backups. Deposit in a repository only with consent.

keyPoints: A good research topic is narrow, feasible, ethical and expressed as a question.
A literature review summarises and judges existing work to identify a gap.
Elicitation uses controlled prompts; natural speech and field notes improve the record.
Informed consent explains purpose, use, storage and the right to withdraw.
Transcription must preserve Yorùbá tone and special letters; annotation adds translation, context and tags.
For counts, percentage = (part ÷ total) × 100; archive with consent, metadata and backups.

en.title: Advanced Yorùbá Phonology and Tone Analysis
en.short: Autosegmental tone, prosody, syllable models, vowel features and small data studies.

sections.heading: Tone as autosegment
sections.text: Autosegmental phonology treats tone as a separate tier. A high (H) or low (L) tone is an autosegment linked to a tone-bearing unit (TBU), usually a vowel or syllabic nasal, by association lines. The Obligatory Contour Principle (OCP) forbids adjacent identical tones on the tone tier, so a model may delete or merge one. Yorùbá has H, mid (M) and L; M is often unmarked in spelling. Ask what an analysis assumes: is M a feature or the absence of tone, and what is the TBU? These choices change predictions.

sections.heading: Prosody and syllables
sections.text: Prosody places tone in a hierarchy: syllable, foot, phonological word and phrase. Tone may spread, delete or stay floating when a vowel is lost. Onset-rime and moraic models both describe Yorùbá (C)V syllables and syllabic nasals, but they divide responsibility for tone differently. Small case: data show H-L on two syllables, and a rule spreads L to the next vowel. Predicted output: H-L-L. If recorded data give H-H-L, the rule is wrong or its domain narrower. Check transcription and domain.

sections.heading: Vowel features
sections.text: Vowel features are used to describe contrasts and harmony. Analyses may use [high], [back], [round], [ATR] and [nasal], with underspecification leaving predictable features blank. Yorùbá has seven oral vowels and nasal vowels; the exact feature set and the treatment of vowel harmony are debated. Autosegmental, metrical and constraint-based models such as Optimality Theory make different predictions. Compare them on the same data rather than accepting a model because it is current.

sections.heading: Small data studies
sections.text: For a small study, choose one question, such as whether a tone spreads across a word boundary. Collect controlled tokens from several speakers, record them, and transcribe tone carefully. Use minimal pairs where possible. Code each token for tone, syllable type and context, then test the model’s prediction. Report variation and limitations. A critical reader checks the data source, transcription, assumed TBU, and whether the conclusion follows.

keyPoints: Autosegmental phonology represents tone on a separate tier linked to tone-bearing units.
The OCP bans adjacent identical tones on the tone tier and motivates deletion or merging.
Yorùbá has H, M and L tones; analyses must state whether M is a feature or absence.
Prosodic domains and syllable models determine where spreading and deletion apply.
Vowel features such as [high], [back], [round], [ATR] and [nasal] are debated in Yorùbá analyses.
Small data studies test a model’s predictions against controlled, carefully transcribed tokens.

en.title: Advanced Syntax and Semantics of Yorùbá
en.short: Formal syntax and semantics: argument structure, focus, quantification, tense and aspect in Yorùbá.

sections.heading: Frameworks and argument structure
sections.text: Advanced work compares theories on the same Yorùbá data. The Minimalist Program builds phrases by Merge and Move. Lexical-Functional Grammar (LFG) separates constituent structure (c-structure) from functional structure (f-structure). Head-driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG) is constraint-based; Construction Grammar works with constructions. Argument structure is a verb’s set of participants, described by theta roles and valency. Lexicalist theories list verb entries; constructionist theories let sentence patterns add meaning. Yorùbá serial verb constructions test both views. In 'Ó gbé é wá' ('he brought it'), two verbs share subject and object. Is this one predicate or two clauses? A formal account must state the sharing and the aspect marking.

sections.heading: Focus and quantification
sections.text: Focus highlights new or contrastive information. Yorùbá often uses the particle ni with a resumptive pronoun: 'Adé ni ó ra ìwé' ('It is Adé who bought a book'). Is the focused phrase moved to a focus phrase, or base-generated with ni as a copula? Alternative semantics (Rooth) treats focus as introducing alternatives; truth-conditional semantics asks what is asserted and presupposed. Quantifiers such as gbogbo ('all') interact with focus and scope. Does gbogbo take wide scope over negation? Test with entailments, not intuition alone.

sections.heading: Tense, aspect and comparison
sections.text: Tense locates an event in time; aspect describes its internal shape, such as completion or progress.
