Yorùbá is often called aspect-prominent, with auxiliaries and tone doing work that inflection does elsewhere. Competing analyses ask whether tense is a syntactic head, a pragmatic inference, or both. Formal semantics uses event variables and temporal relations: an event e is located relative to speech time. The analyst must show how particles, tone and context combine. Critical comparison checks each theory against the same Yorùbá data and its predictions for negation, focus and quantification.

keyPoints: Minimalism, LFG, HPSG and Construction Grammar differ in architecture; compare them on the same Yorùbá data.
Argument structure concerns valency and theta roles; Yorùbá serial verb constructions test lexicalist and constructionist accounts.
Focus in Yorùbá often involves ni and a resumptive pronoun; movement and base-generation analyses compete.
Alternative semantics models focus as alternatives; quantifier scope must be tested with entailments.
Tense and aspect in Yorùbá are marked by auxiliaries, tone and context; their syntactic status is debated.
A formal analysis must predict grammaticality and truth conditions, not just describe one example.

en.title: Theories of Yorùbá Literary and Cultural Criticism
en.short: Applying literary and cultural theory to Yorùbá oral and written texts, including power, gender, performance and canon.

sections.heading: Theory and text
sections.text:
Criticism asks what a text means, how it works and for whom. Formalism, or close reading, studies pattern: image, repetition, structure. It is strong on craft, weak on history. Cultural criticism asks how power, language and institutions shape writing and reading. A reading uses theory as a question, not a label.

Take an oríkì praise poem. A formalist notes repeated epithets and balance. A performance scholar studies voice, drumming and audience reply. A postcolonial critic asks how recording and translation changed it. A feminist critic asks who is praised, by whom, and whose voice is missing. These readings compete; the student should test which explains most.

sections.heading: Postcolonial questions
sections.text: Postcolonial theory studies how colonial rule and its afterlives shape texts, languages and reading. It asks who is represented, who speaks, and which languages carry authority. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) argued that Western writing often produced the East as an object of knowledge. In Yorùbá studies, similar questions arise about colonial grammars, translations and school syllabi. But postcolonial theory can flatten local differences, so check specific Yorùbá institutions and audiences.

sections.heading: Gender and performance
sections.text: Feminist criticism examines how texts imagine men and women, and how gender shapes access to speech and publication. It also asks whether criticism itself repeats male-centred assumptions. Performance theory treats oral texts as events: the performer, audience, place and occasion co-create meaning. A written play can also be studied as performance through staging and reception. These approaches disagree about whether meaning lies in text, context or audience.

sections.heading: Reception and canon
sections.text: Reception theory asks how actual readers and audiences make sense of texts, and how their expectations change. Canon formation is the process by which some texts become central in syllabi, prizes and criticism. A canon is not natural; it reflects institutions, markets and power. Compare a popular oral genre with a school anthology: selection, translation and examination needs can lift one text and silence another. No single theory explains all; use several and state your criteria.

keyPoints: Formalism reads pattern in the text; cultural criticism reads power and context.
Postcolonial criticism asks how colonial rule and its afterlives shape language, representation and reading.
Feminist criticism examines gender in representation and in access to speech and publication.
Performance theory treats oral texts as events shaped by performer, audience and occasion.
Reception theory studies how actual audiences interpret texts and how expectations change.
Canon formation is institutional and political, not natural.

en.title: Research Methods and Dissertation Writing in Yorùbá Studies
en.short: Research design, corpus and fieldwork, data ethics, thesis writing and publication in Yorùbá studies.

sections.heading: Question to design
sections.text: A defensible dissertation begins with a question narrow enough to answer with the time and evidence available. Turn a broad interest into a question: not Yorùbá oral poetry, but how radio presenters in Ibadan choose proverbs for youth programmes. State the gap, the key concepts and the evidence needed. A conceptual framework explains the ideas you will use. A feasible design names sites, participants, sources, methods and limits. Decide whether the question is descriptive, explanatory or interpretive, because each calls for different evidence.

sections.heading: Corpus and fieldwork
sections.text: Corpus methods collect a principled set of texts or recordings. Define the boundary: period, genre, speakers, programme or archive. Fieldwork methods include interviews, focus groups, participant observation and elicitation, which means asking speakers to produce or judge forms. Explain your sampling: why these speakers, sites or texts and not others. Record, label files and keep a transcription convention. In Yorùbá data, tone marks and special letters must be consistent; if unsure of a spelling, mark it for checking rather than guess. Triangulation compares two or more sources to strengthen a claim.

sections.heading: Data, ethics, writing
sections.text: Manage data with a plan: file names, backups, access rules, consent forms and metadata, which is information about each recording or text. Anonymise where promised. Ethics approval and informed consent are normally required; community permission may also be needed for recordings, performances or sacred material. Do not publish what was given in confidence. The thesis is an argument, not a report: each chapter should advance the case. The literature review shows the gap; the methodology chapter justifies choices and states limitations. Use consistent referencing style.

sections.heading: Defence and publication
sections.text: Before submission, check the thesis against your department’s regulations and word limits. The viva, or oral defence, tests whether you understand your choices. For publication, choose a journal that fits the topic and read its guidelines. Peer review is independent expert comment. Keep authorship honest, and archive data where rules allow. A published article is usually narrower than the thesis.

keyPoints: A defensible project turns a broad interest into a narrow question and names the evidence needed.
Corpus and fieldwork designs must justify their sampling and keep transcription consistent.
In Yorùbá data, tone marks and special letters need checking, not guessing.
Informed consent, community permission and a data management plan protect participants and evidence.
The thesis is an argument; each chapter should advance the case and state limitations.
Publication follows journal guidelines and peer review, and authorship must be honest.
